content.positioning: Winterbourne plays the chamber repertoire in rooms small enough to hear the players breathe.
content.introduction: Eighteen players, no conductor, and a season built around one composer at a time. The orchestra takes its name from a stream that runs only in winter: present when the ground is full, gone by June, and none the less a river for it.
content.markRationale: Four strokes of a stave with the middle one missing, under the arc of a held note. The gap is the point — a winterbourne is defined by the part of the year it is absent.
content.colourRationale: Slate carries everything and Paper is warm rather than white, because the programmes are printed on uncoated stock and a cold white would fight it. Sedge is for surfaces. Quill marks the one thing on a page that matters and never more than four percent of it.
content.typeRationale: The logotype is set in the display face and outlined, so the wordmark and the headline of a programme note are the same drawing. This is a typographic identity: the typeface is not a supporting decision, it is the decision.
misuse: Do not set the name in a substitute face. The wordmark is artwork; the licensed face sets everything else.
Do not stretch. Scale both axes together, always.
Do not close the gap in the stave. The absence is the mark.
Do not put Quill behind text. It is there to be the loudest thing on a page, once.
Do not recolour outside the approved colourways.
Do not place the mark on low contrast. Use the reversed lockup.
content.constructionNotes: The stave strokes sit on a seven unit stroke at 17 unit centres, the outer pair shortened by twelve units. The arc is struck at 1.6 times the mark width, crossing the top quarter. Everything is a whole fraction of the 120 unit box.
